reference_answer:
The student's universal claim is false. The parenthetical 'compact, with Haar measure' also needs an explicit qualification: compactness does not make an arbitrary abstract representation continuous or its coefficient functions Haar-integrable. I am assessing that omitted qualification, not assuming continuity for every representation in the question. The requested counterexample can even be continuous and two-dimensional over C.

For a finite group acting linearly on a finite-dimensional complex V, start with any positive-definite Hermitian form h and put h_G(v,w)=|G|^(-1) sum_g h(rho(g)v,rho(g)w). It is sesquilinear and Hermitian, and positive definite because every term at nonzero v is positive. Right reindexing g->gk proves h_G(rho(k)v,rho(k)w)=h_G(v,w). Thus every action map is unitary for h_G. If W is invariant, then for u in W-perp and w in W, h_G(rho(k)u,w)=h_G(u,rho(k)^(-1)w)=0, so W-perp is invariant too. In finite dimension V=W direct_sum W-perp. Induction on dimension gives complete reducibility. Over arbitrary fields the algebraic finite-group complement theorem instead needs the group order invertible in the field; the positive Hermitian/unitary argument is not a modular-characteristic theorem.

The corresponding positive compact statement is conditional: let G be a compact topological group in the usual Haar setting and let rho:G->GL_C(V) be a CONTINUOUS finite-dimensional representation. With normalized bi-invariant Haar probability m, define h_G(v,w)=integral_G h(rho(g)v,rho(g)w) dm(g). The coefficient functions are continuous and bounded, hence integrable. For fixed v!=0, the positive continuous function h(rho(g)v,rho(g)v) has a strictly positive minimum on the compact group, because each rho(g) is invertible, so its integral is positive. Right invariance proves action invariance as above. Orthogonal complements and the same finite-dimensional induction supply the conclusion. Haar existence is an external mathematical input stated by the cited source, not proved here. Source Definition3.38 explicitly includes continuity; that convention was not present among this QA's empty standing fields, and is not silently imported here.

A general infinite group has no finite uniform sum. For the specific noncompact group(R,+), there is no translation-invariant Borel probability measure: all half-open intervals[n,n+1) have the same mass c. If c>0 their disjoint union has infinite mass; if c=0 their countable union R has mass0, contradicting probability1. In other settings one must specify topology, measure and coefficient integrability rather than write1/|G|. These are conditions of this particular normalized sum/Haar construction, not necessary conditions for each representation to be unitarizable. A trivial representation of R is already unitary, for example. No statement here excludes other averaging methods under additional hypotheses.

For the explicit counterexample let N=[[0,1],[0,0]], G=(R,+) and rho(t)=I+tN on C². Since N²=0, rho(s)rho(t)=I+(s+t)N=rho(s+t), rho(0)=I and rho(t)^(-1)=rho(-t); the entries depend continuously on t. The line W=C e1 is invariant. Any vector-space complement in dimension2 must be a line C(a,b) with b!=0. If it were invariant, rho(t)(a,b)=(a+t b,b)=lambda_t(a,b). The second coordinate gives lambda_t=1, and t=1 in the first gives b=0, a contradiction. Indeed W is the only invariant line: the same calculation excludes every line with b!=0. Thus the representation is not irreducible, yet cannot be a direct sum of two invariant lines, so it is not completely reducible. If an invariant positive-definite Hermitian form existed, its W-perp would give the forbidden invariant complement. Hence rho is not unitarizable. Equivalently as a separate check, the squared norm of rho(t)e2=t e1+e2 in any fixed positive form has a positive quadratic t² coefficient, so cannot be constant for all real t.

Compactness ALONE can also fail for abstract representations, without contradicting the continuous compact theorem. Choose irrational alpha and a Q-linear map L:R->R with L(1)=0 and L(alpha)=1 by extending the independent set{1,alpha} to a Hamel basis. It induces an additive well-defined ell:R/Z->R by ell([x])=L(x), since L vanishes on integers. The circle R/Z is compact with its usual topology. Set sigma([x])=I+ell([x])N on C². This is a linear group representation; at[alpha] it has the same nontrivial shear and the preceding complement obstruction, so it is neither completely reducible nor unitarizable. It is not continuous: ell([n alpha])=n is unbounded on a compact domain, whereas a continuous matrix coefficient would be bounded. The algebraic construction uses basis choice and is not an effective algorithm. Nor may its coefficients be integrated by fiat: if ell were Haar-L1, translation by[alpha] and invariance would imply integral ell=integral(ell+1)=integral ell+1, impossible. I make no unproved assertion here about automatic continuity of merely measurable homomorphisms; continuity is a sufficient explicit hypothesis for the positive averaging proof, and other regularity/integrability variants need their own theorem.

Finally, 'not completely reducible' and 'not unitarizable' are two separately proved properties of these shears, not generally equivalent predicates. The one-dimensional representation of Z with n acting by2^n is irreducible and completely reducible, but cannot preserve any positive norm because its generator multiplies every norm by2. The examples above concern finite-dimensional spaces, where subspaces are closed and all positive norms are equivalent. In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert formulation, orthogonal-complement decompositions concern CLOSED invariant subspaces; the algebraic versus closed-subspace notions and bounded/continuous action must be distinguished. No infinite-dimensional Hilbert decomposition, measurable-representation theorem, circuit/resource certificate or local Lean result is supplied by this answer.

exposition.core_summary: The R-shear has an invariant line with no invariant complement, so it is neither completely reducible nor unitarizable. Finite averaging and continuous finite-dimensional compact Haar averaging work; compactness alone for an abstract representation and complete reducibility alone do not imply unitarizability.
